v.why: At very small learning rates the network is under-trained in 243 epochs, so raising the rate helps much more than it does elsewhere.
Rates near 0.278 to 1 make Adam diverge, so increasing the rate further hurts compared with the low or mid band.
With a tiny learning rate, a bigger batch means fewer updates and more under-training.
Moving from very noisy batches of 4 to 10 to somewhat larger ones stabilizes training, whereas at large sizes it adds little or costs updates.
Capacity is the bottleneck at 16 to 40 units, so widening helps more than when the net is already wide.
Deeper networks are less stable at high learning rates, so extra depth worsens divergence.
Strong L2 at 0.129 to 1 causes underfitting, whereas small alpha changes are almost neutral.
Smaller batches add gradient noise and more steps at an already unstable high learning rate.
Wider layers give larger effective updates, which are more prone to blow up at a high learning rate.
A small batch already means many noisy updates, so a higher learning rate pushes training toward instability.
